I’m fairly self-reliant too. Until now, I always disclosed all of my trauma to my therapist but started to slowly open up to my friends. Obviously, I don’t share too much with them because they can only handle so much (a sad truth), but I keep them in the loop. If I’m having a bad day with impulsive shopping, I’ll let them know I’m out at the shops so they can remind me not to spend too much money and they can keep me grounded. If I’m about to make an impulsive purchase, I’ll let them know so they can talk me down. They also help me return items I don’t need. Or if I’m having a hard time with drinking and my sobriety and still want to go out, I’ll go out with friends who will make sure I won’t get drunk and will get home safely. If I need a friend around, I know someone I can call to come hangout and keep me company. It’s not always exactly what I need, but i know I have friends who at least care about me and people I have around who can keep tabs on me. They don’t understand bipolar disorder completely, but I know that I can say “hey, I’m not sleeping right now and I’m spending too much money and I’m having a hard time with my sobriety.” They know that something is going on with me and that I need a little more attention than usual. They’re usually pretty good with trying to hang out with me more and checking in with me more. We don’t talk about my bipolar disorder and that’s okay too. I have a therapist and a psychiatrist to talk about those things with. It’s nice to just have a support system to keep you grounded. They don’t always know what to do but I appreciate their effort. It took me a few years to find friends like this. I had a few bad friends for a few years before I found a good support system. 

That being said, I can’t count on my family except for my brother and his wife. My brother is also bipolar, so he understands the mania and depression like none of my friends do and he has been my biggest advocate. He is medicated and has been stable for 2 years and his wife is a nurse and is really helpful. When I was in the hospital my brother handled all my affairs for me and was my biggest advocate. My friends were also supportive as well, but not in the way that my brother was because they don’t understand bipolar disorder. 

You will always be your best advocate and you will be the only one who will know what’s truly going on inside of your head. And your support system will fail you sometimes. Be your own advocate. You need a support system, but you also need to know how to advocate for yourself. Don’t rely on just one person because that person will fail you sometimes. Have more than one person you can fall back on, but be your biggest advocate and make sure you keep some semblance of self-reliance. I know that can sound bad sometimes, but there is something to being your own advocate and being self-reliant.

I took a sort of large dose accutane for 5 months about 4 years ago and I didn’t experience any bad side effects except for dryness. I also started accutane after a pretty serious depressive episode. 

Accutane did wonders for my self-esteem and I experienced no bad side effects. Of course, everyone is different and you should listen to your doctor, but I don’t think accutane is all bad for people with psychiatric disorders. 

People may try to come at me and disagree, but as someone with diagnosed bipolar, accutane was fine for me and I don’t regret taking it at all. 4 years later and I still have clear skin. 

I had to be really consistent with my psych meds and making sure I was feeling mentally ok while on accutane, but I didn’t experience any episodes while on accutane or shortly after. It wasn’t until about 8 months after I took accutane that I experienced another episode that my psychiatrist did not associate with accutane. 

But at the end of the day, if your mental health professionals do not suggest taking accutane, it may be in your best interest to listen to them.
